name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
aliases: Painting the target around the bullet hole
statement: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is drawing the target after the shots have landed, then reporting the pattern as though it had been predicted in advance.
meaning: This is a fault in the order of operations rather than in a mind. A hypothesis chosen after the data are seen has already used up the evidence that would test it, so the p value attached to it no longer means what it says. The barn wall is the space of comparisons that could have been made: subgroups, outcome measures, exclusion rules, the boundaries of a map, the window of years. Fixing those before looking makes one shot count. Choosing them after looking makes the hit certain and uninformative. The fallacy is methodological, and most of the evidence for it comes from statistical practice rather than from experiments on people. It overlaps with the clustering illusion, which is about perceiving groupings in random data, and with apophenia, which has its own entry. The sharpshooter is the further step of building a claim on the grouping and presenting it as a prediction.

origin.note: Grufferman's paper on clustering in Hodgkin's disease is the earliest use in the scientific literature identified by the etymologist Barry Popik, who quotes it as describing 'the Texas sharpshooter who would shoot his rifle at the side of a barn and then carefully draw a target around each bullet-hole'. The paper itself was not obtained for this entry, and its existence, journal, volume and pages were confirmed at Crossref rather than by reading it. The story is older than the Texan. John Venn's Logic of Chance gives it in 1866 without the name, and the phrase 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy' is dated by Popik to 1992. Kenneth Rothman's 1990 address to a conference on disease clusters is the source Goodman and colleagues take the metaphor from.

evidence: Cancer clusters are the case with the most counting behind it. Goodman and colleagues reviewed 428 publicly available US cluster investigations from January 1990 to September 2011, covering 567 cancer sites or categories of community concern. An increase in incidence was confirmed for 72 of them, 13%. Three were linked to a hypothesised exposure with varying degrees of certainty, and one investigation revealed a clear cause. Their conclusion is that extensive efforts to find causes of community cancer clusters have not been successful. They estimate upwards of 1,000 to 2,000 inquiries about perceived clusters in a given year, most of them about cancer. They name the structural fault as the reactive nature of the study, working from data towards a hypothesis rather than the other way round. It is there that they quote Rothman's sharpshooter, 'who first fires his bullet and only then draws the target'. The arithmetic underneath is the multiple comparisons problem. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn simulated four ordinary analytic choices and reported the false-positive rate each produces at p < .05. Flexibility between two dependent variables correlated at r = .50 gives 9.5%. Adding ten observations per cell and testing again gives 7.7%. Controlling or not controlling for gender gives 11.7%, and dropping one of three conditions gives 12.6%. Used together they give 61%. The same paper reports two real experiments on University of Pennsylvania undergraduates. Thirty heard either a children's song or a control track, and those given the children's song felt older, F(1, 27) = 5.06, p = .033. In the second, 20 participants who heard 'When I'm Sixty-Four' came out nearly a year and a half younger by their stated birth dates than those given the control, F(1, 17) = 4.92, p = .040. The paper then discloses its own workings. Thirty-four undergraduates were run across three conditions and 20 across two were reported, and the age result disappears without father's age as a covariate, F(1, 18) = 1.01, p = .33. Gelman and Loken's contribution is that none of this requires fishing. A researcher who runs a single analysis can still be in a garden of forking paths, because a different data set would have prompted a different but equally defensible analysis. The p value is a statement about what would have happened across data sets, and that is what the contingency destroys. They work through four published claims on that basis. One is a 2013 survey reporting that 40% of women in relationships supported Mitt Romney during the ovulatory phase against 23% at other times. Another reports that women at peak fertility were three times more likely to wear red or pink shirts. They also cite Nosek, Spies and Motyl, whose own replication of a large effect linking political extremism to seeing images as black or white returned p = 0.59, having had a 99% chance of reaching p < .05 on the original estimate. Silberzahn and colleagues put the forking directly on show. Twenty-nine teams of 61 analysts were given one data set and one question, whether football referees give more red cards to dark-skin-toned players. Estimates ran from 0.89 to 2.93 in odds-ratio units with a median of 1.31, twenty teams found a statistically significant positive effect and nine did not, and the 29 analyses used 21 unique combinations of covariates. Analysts' prior beliefs and their level of expertise did not readily explain the spread, and peer ratings of the analyses did not account for it either. On how often the target moves in practice, John, Loewenstein and Prelec surveyed 5,964 American academic psychologists and got 2,155 responses. Asked whether they had reported an unexpected finding as having been predicted from the start, 27.0% said yes in the control condition and 35.0% under an incentive scheme for truthful answers. Thompson takes the same fallacy into forensic DNA, arguing from casework, informal and naturalistic experiments and analysts' own testimony that criteria for a match get shifted after a suspect's profile is known, which makes matches look more probative than they are.

replication.headline: No experiment measuring how susceptible people are to this fallacy was found. The evidence is about how research is done, not about a tendency that has been given to volunteers to demonstrate. The crowdsourced-analysis demonstration inside that evidence has since been run twice more, in other fields, and the analytic spread appeared again.
replication.detail: Two things exist in place of a replication record. The first is repetition of the crowdsourced-analysis design, which has been run twice since Silberzahn. Botvinik-Nezer and colleagues gave one functional MRI data set and the same nine hypotheses to 70 independent teams, and no two teams chose identical workflows. Breznau and colleagues coordinated 161 researchers in 73 teams testing one hypothesis on one data set, that greater immigration reduces public support for social policies. More than 95% of the variance in their numerical results was left unexplained after coding every identifiable decision in each team's workflow, and researchers' expertise, prior beliefs and expectations barely predicted the variation. The second is before-and-after evidence from fields that changed the order of hypothesis and data. Kaplan and Irvin identified 55 large NHLBI cardiovascular trials funded between 1970 and 2012. Of the 30 published before 2000, 17 (57%) reported a benefit on the primary outcome; of the 25 published after, 2 (8%) did, with a chi-square of 12.2 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.0005. Every post-2000 trial was prospectively registered at clinicaltrials.gov and none of the earlier ones was, and 23% of the earlier publications did not identify a primary outcome at all. Scheel, Schijen and Lakens compared 71 published Registered Reports in psychology, the number available as of November 2018, with a random sample of 152 hypothesis-testing studies from the standard literature. Taking the first hypothesis of each article, positive results ran at 96% in the standard sample and 44% in the Registered Reports. Neither before-and-after comparison is randomised, and both mix the effect of fixing the target with the effect of removing publication bias.

limits: Nothing here measures a person. The search for an experiment on individual susceptibility covered Europe PMC, PubMed, Crossref and general web search, pairing the fallacy with terms for experiments, susceptibility and post hoc hypothesising. Europe PMC returns 37 records for the phrase 'Texas sharpshooter', none of them a study of human subjects. Adjacent work exists on hindsight bias, on perceived randomness and on questionable research practices, and none of it uses this fallacy as its outcome measure. Two documents central to the name were not obtained: Grufferman's 1977 paper, which is quoted here from Popik's etymological trace, and Rothman's 1990 conference address, which has no abstract and is quoted here through Goodman and colleagues. Venn's barn-door passage was read in the third edition of 1888 at Project Gutenberg; Wagenmakers places it at page 259 of the 1866 first edition, which was not checked. The cluster figures describe what investigations concluded, not the true rate of environmental causes, and a study that fails to find a cause has not shown there was none. The two before-and-after comparisons in the replication field are observational, and the trial result is confined to one funder and one disease area. The three crowdsourced-analysis studies measure how much analysts' choices move an estimate, not whether any analyst drew a target afterwards. Botvinik-Nezer and Breznau were read as their abstracts. Thompson's paper was read only as its abstract at the publisher, and Evers's editorial only as a summary of its opening.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat any post hoc analysis as the fallacy. Exploring data is how hypotheses are found, and Gelman and Loken say plainly that refining a hypothesis in light of data is good scientific practice. The fallacy is the claim of confirmatory strength for a target drawn afterwards, which is a claim about what the number means rather than about how it was obtained. A second error runs the other way, reading the fallacy as an accusation of cheating. Gelman and Loken's whole argument is that a researcher who performs one honest analysis, with no fishing and no intent, produces an invalid p value whenever a different data set would have led to a different analysis. Silberzahn's 29 teams were experts working in the open and still spread from 0.89 to 2.93. Preregistration is then read as a complete fix. It fixes one target. Gelman and Loken argue it cannot be a general solution, since much observational work in social science and public health cannot realistically be preregistered. Their own recommendation is to analyse all the comparisons rather than one. The name is also taken more literally than it deserves. Popik's trace turns up no actual marksman, and Wagenmakers places the story in Venn in 1866 with no Texas in it. Cancer clusters attract the last confusion. The finding that few investigations identify a cause is a statement about what the method can resolve, given small numbers and boundaries drawn after the cases are known. It is not a verdict on any particular community's suspicion.

sources.text: Grufferman, S. (1977). Clustering and aggregation of exposures in Hodgkin's disease. Cancer, 39(S4), 1829-1833. Not obtained; cited for the earliest use of the sharpshooter story in the scientific literature, with the wording taken from Popik. Journal, volume and pages confirmed at Crossref.
Popik, B. Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy. The Big Apple. Etymological trace giving the 1977 Grufferman quotation, 'Texas sharpshooter effect' in 1982 and 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy' in 1992.
Venn, J. (1888). The Logic of Chance, 3rd edition. Chapter XIV, Fallacies. The barn-door passage was read in the Project Gutenberg transcription of this edition.
Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2018). Origin of the Texas Sharpshooter. Bayesian Spectacles, 11 January. Traces the metaphor to Venn's first edition of 1866, page 259, and to a related passage in Cicero.
Rothman, K. J. (1990). A sobering start for the cluster busters' conference. American Journal of Epidemiology, 132(supp1), 6-13. No abstract; not obtained. Quoted here through Goodman et al. (2012).
